Real idea. Real pushback. Honest results.

7 min read
Just now

--

Business development mind map made by BuildpadI don’t romanticize the startup world. I build things on my own now, freelance AI automation, no-code workflows, tools I’ve needed and couldn’t find. So when Buildpad reached out and offered me credits to test their product, I wasn’t going in as a first-time founder with stars in my eyes.
I went in as someone who knows AI tools well enough to spot the difference between genuine intelligence and a glorified yes-machine.
I brought a real idea. One I’d actually lived.
The Idea: A Problem I’d Hit Myself
Anyone who’s run a content site knows the pain. You hit 100 pages, maybe 200, and suddenly internal linking becomes a nightmare. Not just tedious, genuinely strategic, and the kind of thing that quietly tanks your SEO when you ignore it.
I’d felt this firsthand running a blog. So I brought Buildpad an idea I’d already been turning over: an automated internal linking WordPress plugin, powered by an n8n backend and an LLM, that doesn’t just suggest links but inserts them directly into pages with no manual step required.
I typed it in and hit enter. What happened next is what I want to walk you through.
It Didn’t Just Accept My Idea. It Interrogated It.
The first thing Buildpad did was ask questions to understand me, my idea, and my goal better. Not surface-level ones either.
What kind of website was I running? How many pages before it became painful? Had I tried existing tools, and if so, what did they get wrong?
I told it I’d tried Link Whisper, LinkBoss, and a few others. The problem wasn’t that they didn’t exist, it was that they only recommended links. You still had to go page by page and click.
And the anchor text they suggested was usually pulled from whatever phrase happened to be nearby in the source content, not from what the destination page was actually about.
The agent listened, gathered context, then did something I didn’t expect.
Then It Built the Roadmap
This is the part that genuinely surprised me.
After gathering context in the initial phase, Buildpad didn’t just say “good luck, here are some tips.” Instead, it used its Ultraplan feature, a strategic planning agent, to assess my project and build a structured Roadmap taking me through validation, building, launching, and marketing the product: my whole business journey broken down into concrete phases with specific actions at each step.
Buildpad roadmapLooking at it laid out like that, it stopped feeling like an idea and started feeling like a real project. There’s something about seeing your concept broken into an actual execution plan that shifts how seriously you take it.
But the Roadmap isn’t just something it hands you and walks away from.
It Stays With You Through Every Step
This is what I didn’t expect going in. At each phase of the Roadmap, Buildpad is still there. You hit a challenge, you bring it back, and it helps you work through it. If something changes, if your target customer shifts or your technical approach pivots, it adjusts the plan.
For me, this played out around the architecture question. When I explained that users wouldn’t need their own n8n instance because I’d host the automation myself and they’d just connect through the plugin, the agent immediately understood the implications: this was essentially a SaaS with a WordPress plugin as the front door, not just a standalone plugin.
It updated the framing accordingly and flagged what that meant for pricing, support, and onboarding.
That kind of real-time adjustment is where the cofounder framing starts to make sense. It’s not a one-time planning tool. It’s something you’re meant to return to.
Validating My Idea Through Real-World Data
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Image of AI agents during researchTo validate that my idea had genuine potential and was something people actually wanted, it spawned multiple AI agents who each researched a particular part of the market for real demand signals.
They pulled data from Reddit threads, social media discussions, industry reports, competitor reviews, and more. For example, it surfaced one blogger with 280 posts described fixing internal linking manually as “60+ hours of work” and said they “wanted to throw my laptop out the window.” The agent confirmed that Link Whisper has 50,000+ installs at $97 per year, Internal Link Juicer has 20,000+.
The demand was real, documented, and quantified, not just validated by vibes.

This is where Buildpad separates itself from just chatting with an AI. It doesn’t take your word for it. It checks.
Then It Pushed Me on the Business, Not Just the Product
Once the problem was validated, the questions shifted. Who was I building this for? Solo bloggers or SEO agencies?
I said both. It pushed back immediately: starting with both usually means optimizing for neither. Solo bloggers care about price and simplicity. Agencies care about managing multiple sites and reporting. Pick one.
I went with agencies and SEO freelancers, partly because I already have relationships in that world. The agent built on that immediately, noting those freelancers are a direct path to early customers who already feel this pain across multiple client sites.
On pricing, I landed on monthly subscription per site. The agent agreed it matched the agency model cleanly.
What struck me was how the conversation felt less like filling out a form and more like being grilled by someone who actually wanted the idea to succeed. Every time I gave a vague answer, it pressed for specifics. Every time my thinking drifted, it pulled it back.
By the end of this phase, I had something tighter than what I walked in with: a WordPress plugin connected to a hosted n8n backend, LLM-generated anchor text based on destination page context, full automated insertion with no manual approval step, targeting SEO agencies and freelancers, monthly per-site subscription.
Then It Built Me a Landing Page. And I Was Not Expecting This.
I went into the website phase ready to be underwhelmed. AI-generated landing pages are usually generic templates with placeholder copy that you’d never actually publish. I’ve seen enough of them to know what they look like.
What Buildpad produced stopped me.
It wasn’t a template with my product name swapped in. It was a real landing page, with copy that actually explained what the plugin does, why the existing tools fall short, and who it’s built for. The positioning was sharp. The structure was logical. The headline didn’t sound like it was written by a committee.

This was the moment the product clicked for me as a full workflow, not just a research tool. By the time you get to the landing page phase, you’ve already stress-tested the idea, tightened the positioning, and built an execution plan.
So when the copy comes out, it actually reflects all of that thinking. It’s not generic because the input wasn’t generic.
The Marketing Phase: Where I’d Temper Your Expectations
The marketing phase is the weakest part of the product right now.
It focused on organic channels, LinkedIn, Reddit, content positioning. The advice was sound in principle, but the content it generated needed real editing to match a professional voice. And there’s no scheduling or automation integration, so you’re still copying and pasting everything manually.
For a tool that automates so much elsewhere, this gap is noticeable. The distance between “here’s a post to publish” and actually publishing it is where momentum stalls.
The Reddit research feature is the exception. It found threads where my exact target customer was actively describing the problem I’m solving. That’s a useful signal for early outreach, even if the execution still lands on you.
What It Costs and Whether It’s Worth It
$39 per month, with a 3-day free trial available to try it out. For what the Roadmap, the multi-agent market research, and landing page alone deliver, the paid tier is worth it. Replicating that competitive analysis manually would take days, and the landing page alone would cost you hours or a freelancer’s fee.
The structured workflow, with agents that push back, verify, and adjust, is something you could approximate with Claude or another frontier model, but you’d have to build all the scaffolding yourself. Buildpad has already done that.
The Verdict
Buildpad is what I’d call a serious thinking partner, not a hype generator. It challenged my idea, built me an execution roadmap, verified the demand independently, tightened my positioning, and then produced a landing page I could actually use.
The marketing phase needs work. But everything from ideation through to the landing page is genuinely impressive, especially if you’re the kind of person who has ideas but gets stuck turning them into something real.
Go in with a specific problem you’ve actually lived. The sharper your input, the sharper the output. That’s true of any AI tool, but with Buildpad it really shows.
